{{Short description|Aerodynamic theorem}}

In [[aerodynamics]], '''Crocco's theorem''' relates the [[flow velocity]], [[vorticity]], and [[stagnation pressure]] (or [[entropy]]) of a [[potential flow]]. This [[theorem]] gives the relation between the thermodynamics and fluid kinematics. The theorem was first enunciated by [[Alexander Friedmann]] for the particular case of a [[perfect gas]] and published in 1922:<ref>Friedmann A. An essay on hydrodynamics of compressible fluid (Опыт гидромеханики сжимаемой жидкости), [[Saint Petersburg|Petrograd]], 1922, 516 p., [http://books.e-heritage.ru/book/10073889 reprinted] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303235627/http://books.e-heritage.ru/book/10073889 |date=2016-03-03 }} in 1934 under the editorship of [[Nikolai Kochin]] (see the first formula on page 198 of the reprint).</ref>

:<math>\frac{D\mathbf u}{Dt}=T \nabla s-\nabla h</math>

However, usually this theorem is connected with the name of Italian scientist {{ill|Luigi Crocco|it}},<ref>Crocco L. [http://dictionnaire.narod.ru/Crocco-1937.djvu Eine neue Stromfunktion für die Erforschung der Bewegung der Gase mit Rotation]. [[Journal of Applied Mathematics and Mechanics|ZAMM]], Vol. 17, Issue 1, pp. 1–7, 1937. DOI: 10.1002/zamm.19370170103. Crocco writes the theorem in the form <math>\scriptstyle\mathrm{rot}\,\mathbf u\times\mathbf u=T\mathrm{grad}\,S</math> for [[perfect gas]] (the last formula on page 2).</ref> a son of [[Gaetano Crocco]].

Consider an element of fluid in the flow field subjected to translational and rotational motion: because stagnation pressure loss and entropy generation can be viewed as essentially the same thing, there are three popular forms for writing Crocco's theorem:

# Stagnation pressure: <math> \mathbf u \times \boldsymbol \omega =v \nabla p_0 </math> <ref name="Shapiro">Shapiro, Ascher H. "National Committee for Fluid Mechanics Films Film Notes for 'Vorticity,'" 1969. Encyclopædia Britannica Educational Corporation, Chicago, Illinois. (retrieved from http://web.mit.edu/hml/ncfmf/09VOR.pdf (5/29/11)</ref>
# Entropy (the following form holds for plane steady flows): <math> T \frac{ds}{dn} = \frac{dh_0}{dn} +u \omega </math> <ref name="Liepmann">Liepmann, H. W. and Roshko, A. "Elements of Gasdynamics" 2001. Dover Publications, Mineola, NY (eq. (7.33)).</ref>
# Momentum: <math> \frac{\partial \mathbf u}{\partial t} + \nabla \left(\frac{u^2}{2} + h \right) = \mathbf u \times \boldsymbol \omega + T \nabla s + \mathbf{g},</math>

In the above equations, <math> \mathbf u </math> is the flow velocity vector, <math> \omega </math> is the vorticity, <math> v </math> is the specific volume, <math> p_0 </math> is the [[stagnation pressure]], <math> T </math> is [[temperature]], <math> s </math> is specific [[entropy]], <math> h </math> is specific [[enthalpy]], <math> \mathbf{g} </math> is specific [[body force]], and <math> n </math> is the direction normal to the streamlines. All quantities considered (entropy, enthalpy, and body force) are ''specific'', in the sense of "per unit mass".
